## Summary

The gate-snapshot janitor reclaims along **disk-pressure and age axes only**. It has
**no entry-count bound**. On a large, mostly-empty volume every byte-denominated axis
is inert, so a host that produces snapshots faster than the 7-day cold-trim expires
them accumulates entries without limit — and the resulting harm is **filesystem
metadata pressure**, which no existing axis measures.

Observed 2026-08-26: 13,056–14,705 entries under
`$REBAR_GATE_TMPDIR/rebar-gate-snapshots` drove macOS `fseventsd` to **26.3 GB RSS**
and **>150% CPU**, exhausting swap (53,556 MB of 54,272 MB) and pushing load average
to **58** on a 6-performance-core host until GUI applications could no longer launch.
Disk usage was never the binding constraint.

## What already exists (do not rebuild)

`_snapshot/janitor.py` (519 LOC) + `_snapshot/gc_trigger.py` (244 LOC) implement
operation-linked reclamation, shipped for bug `58a3-0756-e470-4b40`
(`undamaged-epidermic-kakarikis`, closed) after a host reached 64,021 entries /
47.24 GiB. **That fix works and is live on the affected host** —
`<store>/gc/last-pass.stamp` mtime `2026-08-26 19:07:20`, entry count fell
14,705 → 13,056 across the pass. This ticket is NOT a duplicate of it (linked
`relates_to`); it is the remaining gap that fix did not cover.

## Evidence: why every axis stayed inert

Defaults at `janitor.py:65-69`, measured against the affected host:

| Axis | Default | Engaged? |
|---|---|---|
| `free_watermark_bytes` | 2 GiB | No — 886 GiB free |
| `free_watermark_pct` | `0` (off) | No |
| `max_bytes` | `0` (off, opt-in) | No |
| `max_age_seconds` | 7 days | Barely |
| **entry count** | **no such axis** | — |

Volume: 1.8 TiB, 886 GiB available, 51% capacity. Sampling 400 of 13,056 entries by
mtime put **every one between 2026-08-18 and 2026-08-26** — inside the 7-day window —
which is why the 19:07 pass reclaimed only ~1,650 entries and stopped.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The janitor gains a **count-denominated** reclamation axis (or an equivalent
   metadata-pressure proxy) that engages **independently of disk headroom**, so a host
   with abundant free space still bounds the store. Configurable, with a documented
   default that is ON — a default of `0`/off reproduces this incident exactly, as
   `max_bytes` did.
2. A test demonstrates the new axis reclaiming on a store that is **under** every
   existing threshold: free space abundant, `max_bytes` off, and every entry newer
   than `max_age_seconds`. That combination is the incident, and no current test
   covers it.
3. The new axis composes with the existing hysteresis (`RECLAIM_TARGET_MARGIN_PCT`)
   rather than re-firing every pass, and respects `grace_seconds` so an entry in
   active use by a concurrent gate is never evicted.
4. Enforcement rides the existing operation-linked trigger — no new daemon, no CI
   dependency (`project.portability`) — and preserves the O(1) stamp-`stat` decision
   discipline: the trigger must NOT enumerate a 13k-entry store to decide whether to
   run.
5. **Verify rather than build** these, which `run_gc` already provides: cleanup on
   gate completion, crash-leak reclamation, and concurrency safety under the
   non-blocking `<store>/gc/lock` flock. Add covering tests only where genuinely absent.
6. An operator-facing note documents the new default and how to tune it, and gives a
   one-off command to reclaim an already-bloated store (existing hosts will not
   self-heal to the new bound on their own).

## Definition of Done

- New axis implemented, defaulted ON, covered by the AC 2 test.
- AC 3 composition/grace behaviour covered by a test.
- No new complexity-baseline or module-size violations (`janitor.py` is 519 LOC
  against a 800 hard cap — a split along existing call-graph seams may be required).
- Operator note landed.

## Notes

Found while triaging a host-wide starvation incident. A second, independent leak on
the same host — orphaned CPU load generators — is tracked separately as
`f3d9-ecd8-df72-4fa1`; the two compounded but have distinct causes and fixes.

Original filing asserted "no retention bound exists". That was wrong and is corrected
above; see the RCA comment for the full disproof.
